implementation_notes: Here the return address never enters the message: a REQ socket's send() generates the routing envelope and the connected REP socket stores it when it recv()s, so its next send() is routed back to that same peer — the address lives inside the socket. cppzmq keeps this to four calls and is the default ZeroMQ realization; choose the ROUTER/DEALER variant instead when the application must address replies explicitly (several services behind one socket, reply forwarding, answering from another thread), and a broker property when the transport is AMQP.

variants.name: ZeroMQ REQ/REP sockets (reply envelope stored by the socket)
variants.idiom_name: ZeroMQ REQ/REP sockets (reply envelope stored by the socket)
variants.implementation_notes: Here the return address never enters the message: a REQ socket's send() generates the routing envelope and the connected REP socket stores it when it recv()s, so its next send() is routed back to that same peer — the address lives inside the socket. cppzmq keeps this to four calls and is the default ZeroMQ realization; choose the ROUTER/DEALER variant instead when the application must address replies explicitly (several services behind one socket, reply forwarding, answering from another thread), and a broker property when the transport is AMQP.
pitfalls: REQ enforces strict send/recv alternation with one outstanding request: a lost reply wedges the socket unless ZMQ_REQ_RELAXED is set.
If the requester is gone, a REP's reply is silently discarded — the socket model has no dead-letter equivalent.
A REP handler that throws or returns without send() leaves the peer blocked, so every path that should answer must be guarded.

variants.name: ZeroMQ ROUTER/DEALER with explicit routing-id envelopes
variants.idiom_name: ZeroMQ ROUTER receiving the routing id as the first frame
variants.implementation_notes: With ROUTER the address is visible to the application: the socket prepends the originating peer's routing id as the first frame, and the service keeps that frame and sends it back (with an empty delimiter frame when the peer is a REQ socket) to route the answer. This is the ZeroMQ realization of the pattern proper — the address travels with the request — and the variant to use when replies are forwarded, buffered or produced by another thread or process.
pitfalls: Routing ids are connection-scoped: a reconnecting peer gets a new id, so a stored id sends the reply to a dead or recycled peer (ROUTER drops it silently).
REQ peers demand the empty delimiter frame; omit it and the reply never matches the request.
ROUTER drops messages for unknown or high-water-marked peers instead of blocking, so the failure is invisible without monitoring.
